newsitem.title: JORDAN: Little cheer for Iraq's fragmented opposition.
newsitem.headline: Little cheer for Iraq's fragmented opposition.

text.p: Iraqi dissidents and opposition groups were united in welcoming U.S. reports last week that President Saddam Hussein faces a serious power struggle in Baghdad.
They all agree Saddam must go.

But beyond a common goal of toppling the man who has led Iraq for quarter of a century, through two disastrous wars and six years of crippling sanctions, the opposition has little to unite it. Geographically and ideologically it is deeply fragmented.

Scattered around Europe and the Middle East, it includes communists and Moslem fundamentalists, Sunnis and Shi'ites, Kurds and Arabs, disaffected government officials and life-long rebels, all with different aims for a post-Saddam Iraq.
Even while Saddam remains in power, his opponents sometimes can't help breaking ranks.
Kurdish faction leader Massoud Barzani requested Saddam's military intervention last August in his long-running feud with rival Kurdish forces led by Jalal Talabani.
Saddam's foray into northern Iraq, semi-autonomous since a Kurdish uprising which followed Baghdad's 1991 Gulf War defeat, didn't just shatter U.S. hopes for a united Kurdish opposition.
It made the region, a backdoor out of Baghdad for disgruntled Iraqis, unsafe for his opponents, undermining even further the chances of coordinated opposition from inside Iraq.
Iraqi dissidents in Baghdad's neighbouring capitals of Tehran, Damascus and Amman or in faraway London were helpless.
So when U.S. officials launched a coordinated rhetorical broadside against Saddam last week the opposition took heart, even if analysts raised eyebrows in surprise at the U.S claims.

Not only had Washington shown it still saw Saddam as a belligerent "demon". It said he faced a power struggle, had put his wife under house arrest, and his powerful eldest son Uday could lose his leg to gangrene after being shot in December.

"It is a signal to the ruling elite and army officers that Saddam has no future and that his status is not stable," said Hamid al-Bayati, spokesman of the Supreme Council for the Islamic Revolution in Iraq.
But even sympathetic observers say the opposition are in no state to capitalise on troubles in Saddam's family.
"They are penetrated, antagonistic to each other, ineffective, and greedy," one Western diplomat said.

He said Saddam's downfall was more likely to be at the hands of a general of the elite Republican Guard or a member of his extended family which makes up Baghdad's inner ruling circle than the scattered opposition.
A candidate with just those credentials emerged when Saddam's son-in-law and weapons mastermind Hussein Kamel turned against him and defected to Jordan two years ago.
But the opposition spurned him, saying his hands were tainted with the same blood as Saddam's.

The December gun and grenade attack on Uday Saddam Hussein also showed how little common ground is shared by the opposition groups. They couldn't agree who shot Uday, or why, or how badly he was injured.

Claims of responsibility came from a tribal spokesman and an Iranian-based Islamist group. His attackers fled variously through Jordan, northern Iraq or Iran, and Uday is now paralysed, sexually impotent, close to death, or all three.
Before the Gulf War of 1991 there were 20 Iraqi opposition groups. The number rose to over 100 in the months that followed with defections of military and political officials.
As well as the Kurdish opposition and the coalition Supreme Council of the Islamic Revolution in Iraq, the Iraqi National Congress forms the third main alliance, grouping 30 factions.
Amman also hosts the Iraqi National Accord, made up mainly of ex-Baathists and government officials.
The Kurds seek a form of expanded autonomy for the northern Kurdish provinces, while the INC and INA have called for a liberal democratic government to replace Saddam's rule.
The SCIRI is a coalition of six Shi'ite fundamentalist groups. Based in Tehran with an army of a few thousand near the Iraqi border, it seeks an Iranian-style Islamic state in Iraq.
